warmup.q: sealed interface Either<out L, out R> with data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing>. In fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.map(f: (R) -> R2): Either<L, R2>, can the Left branch simply return this?
options: No: this is an Either<L, R>, and the function must return an Either<L, R2>
Yes: a Left<L> is an Either<L, Nothing>, which is an Either<L, R2> because Nothing is a subtype of R2 and R is out
Only with an unchecked cast to Either<L, R2>
Only if R2 is the same type as R
warmup.why: After the smart cast, this is a Left<L>, whose declared supertype is Either<L, Nothing>. With out R, Nothing below R2 means Either<L, Nothing> is below Either<L, R2>. So one Left object is a valid result for any success type. Java, with no Nothing, has to build a new Left in that branch.

opening:
Picture the back door of the fruit shop on a busy day. Deliveries arrive from morning to night, and a board of bells hangs by the door, one bell for each kind of delivery. When apples arrive, the apple bell rings, and everyone who asked to hear it comes: the sign-writer, who writes a card for each variety, and the stock-keeper, who counts every fruit of any kind.

Wiring up that board is where people slip. The board keeps one list of listeners per bell, and every list must accept any fruit. The sign-writer only understands apples. Force the sign-writer onto that list with a cast, and it compiles. It even works, until the day a lemon reaches the sign-writer.

Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance ended with that question, and this last lesson of the track answers it with everything since lesson 1. In this lesson, we'll build four small designs: a result that is either a problem or a fruit, a storeroom with a read-only display case, the board of bells, and a container whose keys carry their value's type. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the back door, with a board of bells and a sign-writer who only understands apples. From lesson 1's labeled box on, the whole track went into four designs: an Either whose Left fits every success type, a display case that lets readers in and keeps writers out, a board that keeps narrow listeners behind a checking adapter, and keys that carry their value's type and stay invariant.

Search your code for @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST"). Each one should sit somewhere private, with a comment that says why it's safe by construction.

Next, we'll start a new track, Functional programming in Kotlin, with pure functions, the idea everything else builds on. How can a function have more inputs than parameters?

sections.h: A problem or a fruit: Either, with two out parameters and Nothing
sections.html:
The first design comes from the back door too. Each delivery note is read and checked, and the check has two possible outcomes: a problem ("no weight written") or a good value. A result type that holds exactly one of two kinds of value is often called Either, with a Left for the problem and a Right for the value:

Java
// Java 21: a sealed interface and records. Java has no Nothing, so Left carries an R it never uses.
sealed interface Either<L, R> permits Left, Right {}
record Left<L, R>(L value) implements Either<L, R> {}
record Right<L, R>(R value) implements Either<L, R> {}

static <L, R, R2> Either<L, R2> map(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super R, ? extends R2> f) {
    return switch (e) {
        case Left<L, R> l -> new Left<>(l.value());          // must rebuild: a Left<L, R> is not a Left<L, R2>
        case Right<L, R> r -> new Right<>(f.apply(r.value()));
    };
}
Kotlin
sealed interface Either<out L, out R> {
    data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing>
    data class Right<out R>(val value: R) : Either<Nothing, R>
}

fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.map(f: (R) -> R2): Either<L, R2> = when (this) {
    is Either.Left -> this                                 // no rebuild needed
    is Either.Right -> Either.Right(f(value))
}

Two tools from this track meet here. An Either only hands its values out, so both parameters are out (lesson 4): a dispenser with one of two things inside. And Left fills the unused side with Nothing, lesson 10's box that can never hold anything and so fits every label. Put together, a Left<String> is an Either<String, Nothing>. Because Nothing is a subtype of every type and R is out, it is also an Either<String, R2> for any R2. That's why is Either.Left -> this type-checks: the same problem slip is a valid result for any kind of success. Java has neither tool, so its map must build a new Left every time.

The interface is sealed, which means all its subclasses are declared in the same file. So the compiler knows Left and Right are the only cases, and a when that forgets one is an error. A caller can map the value, fall back with getOrElse, or handle both cases. Unlike an exception, the problem is part of the signature, where every reader sees it.

Covariance makes results combine, too: an Either<String, Long> is an Either<Any, Number>, so a function that reports any problem and any number accepts it. Remove the outs and almost everything breaks at once, including the Left and Right declarations themselves: Type parameter 'L' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position in type 'Either<L (of class Left<out L>), Nothing>'. A supertype is a position too. The demo counts six errors.

With out and Nothing, one Left fits every success type. Return it as it is.

Either only hands values out. The next design hands values out from a type that also takes them in.

try.title: Fold, mapLeft, then remove out
steps: Run EitherDemo and EitherDemoJava. Compare how mapLeft handles the Right branch in each.
In EitherDemo.kt, remove both outs from sealed interface Either (keep the ones on Left and Right). Predict how many lines break, then run.

code.title: EitherDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l11.demo /** Both parameters are out: an Either only hands values out. Left and Right fill the other side with Nothing. */ sealed interface Either<out L, out R> { data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing> data class Right<out R>(val value: R) : Either<Nothing, R> } /** Maps the failure side. `is Right -> this` type-checks because a Right<R> is an Either<Nothing, R>. */ fun <L, R, L2> Either<L, R>.mapLeft(f: (L) -> L2): Either<L2, R> = when (this) { is Either.Left -> Either.Left(f(value)) is Either.Right -> this } fun <L, R, T> Either<L, R>.fold(onLeft: (L) -> T, onRight: (R) -> T): T = when (this) { is Either.Left -> onLeft(value) is Either.Right -> onRight(value) } fun parseGrams(text: String): Either<String, Long> = text.toLongOrNull()?.let { Either.Right(it) } ?: Either.Left("not a number: $text") fun main() { val ok = parseGrams("180") val bad = parseGrams("a handful") println(ok.fold({ "error: $it" }, { "grams: $it" })) println(bad.mapLeft { it.uppercase() }) val wider: Either<Any, Number> = ok // out on both sides: String -> Any, Long -> Number println("wider = $wider") // Break it: remove both `out`s from `sealed interface Either` (keep them on Left and Right), // run, and read the errors in mapLeft and on the `wider` line. }

alt.title: EitherDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java twin of EitherDemo.kt, with a sealed interface and records (Java 21 pattern matching). * Java has no Nothing, so Left must carry an R it never uses, and mapLeft must build a new Right. */ public class EitherDemoJava { sealed interface Either<L, R> permits Left, Right {} record Left<L, R>(L value) implements Either<L, R> {} record Right<L, R>(R value) implements Either<L, R> {} static <L, R, L2> Either<L2, R> mapLeft(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super L, ? extends L2> f) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> new Left<>(f.apply(l.value())); case Right<L, R> r -> new Right<>(r.value()); // can't reuse r: it is an Either<L, R> }; } static <L, R, T> T fold(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super L, ? extends T> onLeft, Function<? super R, ? extends T> onRight) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> onLeft.apply(l.value()); case Right<L, R> r -> onRight.apply(r.value()); }; } static Either<String, Long> parseGrams(String text) { try { return new Right<>(Long.parseLong(text)); } catch (NumberFormatException ex) { return new Left<>("not a number: " + text); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Either<String, Long> ok = parseGrams("180"); Either<String, Long> bad = parseGrams("a handful"); System.out.println(EitherDemoJava.<String, Long, String>fold(ok, l -> "error: " + l, r -> "grams: " + r)); System.out.println(mapLeft(bad, String::toUpperCase)); Either<? extends Object, ? extends Number> wider = ok; // Java: wildcards at the use site System.out.println("wider = " + wider); } }

try.expect: Both print grams: 180, the problem in capitals (Left(value=NOT A NUMBER: A HANDFUL) in Kotlin, Left[value=NOT A NUMBER: A HANDFUL] for the Java record) and wider = Right(value=180). Kotlin's mapLeft returns this for a Right; Java builds a new Right. Without the outs you get six errors: Left and Right themselves (Type parameter 'L' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position ...), mapLeft's when, two in parseGrams, and Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Either<Any, Number>', actual 'Either<String, Long>'.

sections.h: Reading behind glass: a covariant display case on an invariant storeroom
sections.html:
The second design is the storeroom itself. The shop keeps records of its suppliers (the farms that deliver) and its crates, each with an id. A storeroom object can save an item, find one by id and list them all. Because it both takes items in (save) and hands them out (findAll), it must be invariant, like the crate of apples in lesson 3. That hurts the readers. A stock check that wants to list items of any kind can't accept a Storeroom<Supplier, Long> as a Storeroom<Item<Long>, Long>.

The fix is to put the reading half behind glass, as an interface of its own: lesson 3's display case.

Java
interface DisplayCase<T> { List<T> findAll(); }                     // Java: invariant, so...

static void printAll(DisplayCase<? extends Item<?>> display) {      // ...each reader writes ? extends
    for (Item<?> item : display.findAll()) System.out.println("item " + item.getId());
}
Kotlin
interface Item<ID : Comparable<ID>> { val id: ID }

interface DisplayCase<out T> { fun findAll(): List<T> }           // only hands T out

interface Storeroom<T : Item<ID>, ID : Comparable<ID>> : DisplayCase<T> {
    fun save(item: T): T                                           // takes T in: invariant
    fun findById(id: ID): T?
}

fun printAll(display: DisplayCase<Item<*>>) {
    for (item in display.findAll()) println("item ${item.id}")
}

Now printAll accepts the suppliers and the crates, because each storeroom is a DisplayCase of its item type, and the display case is covariant. Unlike lesson 10's display case, this one has no secret slot. The full storeroom is still invariant, and the compiler still refuses val anyItem: Storeroom<Item<Long>, Long> = suppliers with Initializer type mismatch. Nothing was weakened. The safe half simply got its own name.

The bounds are lesson 2's tools. ID : Comparable<ID> lets the lab's storeroom keep its items in a TreeMap, a map that keeps its keys in sorted order. T : Item<ID> ties each item to the type of its id: a Long for suppliers, and a String such as "c-1" for crates. The Kotlin docs give the same advice for any type that both reads and writes: split the interface instead of casting. You'll also hear this called interface segregation, here done by variance.

Notice where the variance came from. You didn't decide that DisplayCase is covariant. You looked at its members, saw that each one only returns T, and the compiler agreed. That's the habit this track has built: read the positions, and let them tell you.

When a type both reads and writes T, give the reading half its own out interface.

Values flow out of the display case. In the third design, values flow out of one side and into the other.

sections.h: The board of bells: deliveries flow out, listeners take them in
sections.html:
The third design is the board from the opening, and the figure shows it. In code it's an event bus: an object that passes each event, a message that something happened, to everyone who asked to hear that kind of event. Here each delivery is the event. Deliveries flow out of the back door, and listeners take them in. That's lessons 4 and 5 in one class:

Java
final class Bells {
    private final List<Consumer<Fruit>> adapters = new ArrayList<>();

    <E extends Fruit> void listen(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> listener) {   // Consumer Super
        adapters.add(item -> {
            if (type.isInstance(item)) listener.accept(type.cast(item));
        });
    }
}
Kotlin
class BellBoard {
    private val bells = HashMap<KClass<out Fruit>, MutableList<(Fruit) -> Unit>>()

    fun <E : Fruit> listen(type: KClass<E>, listener: (E) -> Unit) {
        bells.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() }
            .add { item -> type.safeCast(item)?.let(listener) }     // the adapter
    }

    fun ring(item: Fruit) { bells[item::class]?.forEach { it(item) } }
}

Every piece has a reason. The map's keys are KClass<out Fruit>, because that's the type of item::class, lesson 9's note asked of a value. The listener can't go into the list as it is, and the compiler explains why: Argument type mismatch: actual type is '(E (of fun <E : Fruit> listen)) -> Unit', but '(Fruit) -> Unit' was expected. A listener that only takes apples can't be handed a lemon, because function parameters are in. So the board stores an adapter, a small wrapper that turns one function type into another. It takes any Fruit, checks it with safeCast, and passes on only an E, like a doorman at each bell who reads every delivery note before calling anyone. The same in helps at the call site: the stock-keeper, a (Fruit) -> Unit, can listen under Apple::class.

The shortcut from the opening is to cast the listener instead, .add(listener as (Fruit) -> Unit) under @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST"). It compiles, and erasure makes the cast itself succeed. Then the first lemon that reaches that list throws ClassCastException from inside the sign-writer's own code, far from the line that caused it. The adapter costs one line and turns the wrong delivery into nothing at all.

For Kotlin callers, add the reified wrapper from lesson 8, with one new word:

Java
// Java callers pass the class to the Java board: bells.listen(Apple.class, a -> writeSign(a));
// There is no Java equivalent of the reified, noinline wrapper.
Kotlin
inline fun <reified E : Fruit> listen(noinline listener: (E) -> Unit) = listen(E::class, listener)

board.listen<Apple> { writeSign(it) }

A lambda passed to an inline function is normally inlined too, so it never exists as an object. This one gets stored in the map, so it must stay an object, and noinline says so.

One limit to know: this board rings by the exact class. A listener under Fruit::class never hears anything, because no delivery's run-time class is the interface itself. The "Go deeper" part shows how to walk the supertypes when you need that.

Store a narrow listener behind a checking adapter, never behind a cast.

The last design keeps many kinds of values in one place, and it's the most delicate of the four.

sections.h: Keys that carry their value's type: one container, many types, no casts
sections.html:
The last design is a container for values of many types: the facts the shop keeps about one order, such as the varieties chosen, the weight of each piece and the total weight. Lesson 9's card index used the type as the whole key. Here the key is a small object that carries a name and the full type of its value, like a tab on a card that says both "weights" and "a list of grams":

Java
record Key<T>(String name, Type type) {                         // Type from a super type token
    static <T> Key<T> of(String name, TypeRef<T> ref) { return new Key<>(name, ref.type); }
}
static final Key<List<String>> VARIETIES = Key.of("varieties", new TypeRef<List<String>>() {});

<T> void set(Key<T> key, T value) { values.put(key, value); }
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
<T> T get(Key<T> key) { return (T) values.get(key); }          // safe: only set puts values in
Kotlin
data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType)
inline fun <reified T> key(name: String) = Key<T>(name, typeOf<T>())

val VARIETIES = key<List<String>>("varieties")

operator fun <T> set(key: Key<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value }
@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
operator fun <T> get(key: Key<T>): T? = values[key] as T?     // safe: only set puts values in

val varieties: List<String>? = attributes[VARIETIES]            // no cast, no type argument at the call site

The key's type parameter does the typing. attributes[VARIETIES] is a List<String>?, with no cast at the call site, and attributes[VARIETIES] = 42 is a compile error: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'List<String>' was expected. The KType inside the key makes key<List<Int>>("weights") and key<Int>("weights") different keys. So when two helpers both pick the name "weights", one for the weight of each piece and one for the total, the two values don't land in the same slot.

Key<T> is invariant on purpose, and this is the last variance decision of the track. Declare it out T, and a Key<List<String>> becomes a Key<Any>. Then attributes[VARIETIES] = 42 would compile, with T inferred as Any, and the next read of the varieties throws ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.util.List. The demo's LeakyKey does exactly that. A key is used to write as well as to read, so it can't be a producer, however few members it has. The one unchecked cast in get stays safe only while that holds. It's safe by construction: the only way in is set(key: Key<T>, value: T), and the key can't pretend to be another type.

A key that decides what may be written must be invariant.

This is also a good place to stop adding generics. Four designs, two commented casts, one deliberately invariant key: if a design needs much more than that, a plainer one with a sealed class and a when is usually easier for the next person to read. And know the limit of all four. They check types, not meaning: the compiler will happily file a weight of minus 50 grams under exactly the right key.

try.title: Store typed attributes, then break the key
steps: Run TypedKeysDemo and TypedKeysDemoJava. Neither call site has a cast.
Read LeakyKey in the Kotlin file: the same key with out T. Find the line where the bad value goes in, and the line where it fails.
Uncomment the wrong move in each file. The invariant key stops at compile time what the leaky key let through.

code.title: TypedKeysDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l11.demo import kotlin.reflect.KType import kotlin.reflect.typeOf /** Invariant on purpose: a Key<List<String>> is not a Key<Any>. */ data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType) inline fun <reified T> key(name: String) = Key<T>(name, typeOf<T>()) class Attributes { private val values = HashMap<Key<*>, Any?>() operator fun <T> set(key: Key<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") // safe: only set(Key<T>, T) puts values in operator fun <T> get(key: Key<T>): T? = values[key] as T? } /** The same thing with `out T`: it compiles, and it is broken. */ data class LeakyKey<out T>(val name: String, val type: KType) inline fun <reified T> leakyKey(name: String) = LeakyKey<T>(name, typeOf<T>()) class LeakyAttributes { private val values = HashMap<LeakyKey<*>, Any?>() operator fun <T> set(key: LeakyKey<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") operator fun <T> get(key: LeakyKey<T>): T? = values[key] as T? } val VARIETIES = key<List<String>>("varieties") val TOTAL = key<Int>("total grams") fun main() { val attrs = Attributes() attrs[VARIETIES] = listOf("Gala", "Fuji") attrs[TOTAL] = 330 val varieties: List<String>? = attrs[VARIETIES] // typed by the key: no cast here println("varieties = $varieties, total = ${attrs[TOTAL]} g") val leaky = LeakyAttributes() val leakyVarieties = leakyKey<List<String>>("varieties") leaky[leakyVarieties] = 42 // compiles: T is inferred as Any try { val first: String? = leaky[leakyVarieties]?.first() println(first) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" (")}") } // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // attrs[VARIETIES] = 42 }

alt.title: TypedKeysDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType; import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Java twin of TypedKeysDemo.kt. The key's type comes from a super type token; Java generics are invariant. */ public class TypedKeysDemoJava { static abstract class TypeRef<T> { final Type type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0]; } record Key<T>(String name, Type type) { static <T> Key<T> of(String name, TypeRef<T> ref) { return new Key<>(name, ref.type); } } static final class Attributes { private final Map<Key<?>, Object> values = new HashMap<>(); <T> void set(Key<T> key, T value) { values.put(key, value); } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") // safe: only set(Key<T>, T) puts values in <T> T get(Key<T> key) { return (T) values.get(key); } } static final Key<List<String>> VARIETIES = Key.of("varieties", new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}); static final Key<Integer> TOTAL = Key.of("total grams", new TypeRef<Integer>() {}); public static void main(String[] args) { Attributes attrs = new Attributes(); attrs.set(VARIETIES, List.of("Gala", "Fuji")); attrs.set(TOTAL, 330); List<String> varieties = attrs.get(VARIETIES); // typed by the key: no cast here System.out.println("varieties = " + varieties + ", total = " + attrs.get(TOTAL) + " g"); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // attrs.set(VARIETIES, 42); } }

try.expect: Both print varieties = [Gala, Fuji], total = 330 g. Kotlin then prints ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.util.List: leaky[leakyVarieties] = 42 compiled because out T let T be inferred as Any, and the read failed later. The wrong move fails with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'List<String>' was expected. in Kotlin, and method set in class Attributes cannot be applied to given types in Java.

video.title: Typed keys: the key carries its value's type, so a read needs no cast and same-named keys don't collide, and the key stays invariant because it writes too

compare.title: The board of bells in Java and Kotlin

java.title: BellBoard.java
java.html: import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Consumer; final class BellBoard { private final Map<Class<? extends Fruit>, List<Consumer<Fruit>>> bells = new HashMap<>(); // Consumer<? super E>: a listener for E or for any supertype of E <E extends Fruit> void listen(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> listener) { bells.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(item -> { if (type.isInstance(item)) listener.accept(type.cast(item)); // the adapter }); } int ring(Fruit item) { List<Consumer<Fruit>> listeners = bells.getOrDefault(item.getClass(), List.of()); listeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(item)); return listeners.size(); } } // board.listen(Apple.class, a -> writeSign(a));

kotlin.title: BellBoard.kt
kotlin.html: class BellBoard { private val bells = HashMap<KClass<out Fruit>, MutableList<(Fruit) -> Unit>>() // (E) -> Unit is already Function1<in E, ...>: a listener for any supertype of E fits fun <E : Fruit> listen(type: KClass<E>, listener: (E) -> Unit) { bells.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() } .add { item -> type.safeCast(item)?.let(listener) } // the adapter } inline fun <reified E : Fruit> listen(noinline listener: (E) -> Unit) = listen(E::class, listener) fun ring(item: Fruit): Int { val listeners = bells[item::class] ?: return 0 for (l in listeners) l(item) return listeners.size } } // board.listen<Apple> { writeSign(it) }

compare.note: The design is the same in both languages: keys from the item's run-time class, listeners stored behind an adapter that checks the class and casts, and a listener parameter that accepts supertypes. Where Java writes the variance at each use (Class<? extends Fruit> keys, Consumer<? super E> listeners), Kotlin gets it from declarations: item::class is already a KClass<out Fruit>, and a function type is already in on its parameter, so (E) -> Unit needs no projection. Kotlin also adds the reified wrapper, which needs noinline because the lambda is stored. Java callers can reach the KClass version only through JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(Apple.class), so a board meant for Java code should also offer a Class<E> overload.

worked.title: Receive a delivery note through all four designs

steps.say: A delivery note arrives as a map of text fields, read from a paper form. 1. Parse it into an Either instead of throwing, so the caller decides what a bad note means.
steps.code: fun parseDelivery(note: Map<*, *>): Either<String, Fruit> { val name = note["name"] as? String ?: return Either.Left("missing name") val grams = (note["grams"] as? Number)?.toInt() ?: return Either.Left("missing weight") return when (note["kind"]) { "apple" -> Either.Right(Apple(name, grams)) "lemon" -> Either.Right(Lemon(name, grams)) else -> Either.Left("unknown kind ${note["kind"]}") } }

alt.html: static Either<String, Fruit> parseDelivery(Map<?, ?> note) { if (!(note.get("name") instanceof String name)) return new Left<>("missing name"); if (!(note.get("grams") instanceof Number n)) return new Left<>("missing weight"); int grams = n.intValue(); Object kind = note.get("kind"); if ("apple".equals(kind)) return new Right<>(new Apple(name, grams)); if ("lemon".equals(kind)) return new Right<>(new Lemon(name, grams)); return new Left<>("unknown kind " + kind); }

steps.say: 1. Ring the bell for each good delivery. 3. Record each problem in the day's typed attributes. Self-check before reading the comment: why can Either.Right(Apple(name, grams)) be returned where Either<String, Fruit> is expected? (Right<Apple> is an Either<Nothing, Apple>, and both parameters are out.)
steps.code: val LAST_PROBLEM = key<String>("delivery.lastProblem") fun receive(note: Map<*, *>, board: BellBoard, today: Attributes): Int = when (val parsed = parseDelivery(note)) { is Either.Right -> board.ring(parsed.value) // the item flows out to the listeners is Either.Left -> { today[LAST_PROBLEM] = parsed.value; 0 } }

alt.html: static final Key<String> LAST_PROBLEM = Key.of("delivery.lastProblem", new TypeRef<String>() {}); static int receive(Map<?, ?> note, BellBoard board, Attributes today) { return switch (parseDelivery(note)) { case Right<String, Fruit> r -> board.ring(r.value()); case Left<String, Fruit> l -> { today.set(LAST_PROBLEM, l.value()); yield 0; } }; }

steps.say: 1. Wire the listeners once, when the shop opens. The stock-keeper is a (Fruit) -> Unit and listens under both kinds; the sign-writer only understands apples. A nightly report lists the suppliers through the covariant DisplayCase<Item<*>>. Every type parameter in this flow has the variance its role demands, and the only casts are the two that are safe by construction: safeCast in the board's adapter, and the unchecked cast inside Attributes.get.
steps.code: val stockCount: (Fruit) -> Unit = { stock.add(it.name, it.grams) } board.listen(Apple::class, stockCount) board.listen(Lemon::class, stockCount) board.listen<Apple> { signs.write(it.name) } receive(mapOf("kind" to "apple", "name" to "Gala", "grams" to 180), board, today) // 2 listeners ran receive(mapOf("kind" to "apple", "name" to "Fuji"), board, today) // today[LAST_PROBLEM] == "missing weight"

alt.html: Consumer<Fruit> stockCount = f -> stock.add(f.getName(), f.getGrams()); board.listen(Apple.class, stockCount); board.listen(Lemon.class, stockCount); board.listen(Apple.class, a -> signs.write(a.getName())); receive(Map.of("kind", "apple", "name", "Gala", "grams", 180), board, today); // 2 listeners ran receive(Map.of("kind", "apple", "name", "Fuji"), board, today); // LAST_PROBLEM is "missing weight"

lab.title: Build Either, a storeroom, a board of bells and typed keys
steps: Run the tests. All thirteen fail. Work through the files in order; each part has its own tests.
Either.kt (a TODO in each of two functions): write map with is Either.Left -> this, and getOrElse.
Storeroom.kt (TODOs 1 to 3): add out to DisplayCase. Back InMemoryStoreroom with a java.util.TreeMap<ID, T>. Write saveAll and describeAll.
BellBoard.kt (TODOs 4 to 6): store an adapter in listen, make the one-argument listen inline with a reified E and a noinline listener, and write ring so it returns the number of listeners that ran.

Attributes.kt (TODOs 7 and 8): make key inline and reified with typeOf<T>(), then write set, get, getOrDefault and remove. Use key in values for getOrDefault, so a stored null is not mistaken for a missing key.
Run until all thirteen pass. Then remove out from DisplayCase once more and watch which test turns red.
hints: A TreeMap works as byId[item.id] = item, and byId.values.toList() is already in id order.
The adapter is bells.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() }.add { item -> type.safeCast(item)?.let(listener) }. safeCast needs import kotlin.reflect.safeCast.
ring: val listeners = bells[item::class] ?: return 0, then call each one and return listeners.size.
Each unchecked cast in Attributes needs @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST"). Write one comment that says why it's safe: only set(key: Key<T>, value: T) puts values in, and Key is invariant.

drill.title: Write Either and map from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write Either with Left and Right in Kotlin, with the variance and the Nothing that let map return this for a Left. Write map. Then write the Java version with a sealed interface and records, and point at the line where Java has to build a new object.

answer.html: sealed interface Either<out L, out R> { data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing> data class Right<out R>(val value: R) : Either<Nothing, R> } fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.map(f: (R) -> R2): Either<L, R2> = when (this) { is Either.Left -> this // Either<L, Nothing> is an Either<L, R2> is Either.Right -> Either.Right(f(value)) }

alt.title: Either.java
alt.html: sealed interface Either<L, R> permits Left, Right {} record Left<L, R>(L value) implements Either<L, R> {} record Right<L, R>(R value) implements Either<L, R> {} static <L, R, R2> Either<L, R2> map(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super R, ? extends R2> f) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> new Left<>(l.value()); // here: no Nothing, so a new Left case Right<L, R> r -> new Right<>(f.apply(r.value())); }; }

recap: Either<out L, out R> with Left : Either<L, Nothing> lets one Left stand for every success type, so map can return this. Java must rebuild it.
When a type both reads and writes T, give the reading half its own out T interface, the display case. Readers get covariance; the full storeroom stays invariant and safe.

On a board of bells, deliveries are produced and listeners consume. Keys are KClass<out Fruit> from item::class, listeners sit behind a safeCast adapter rather than a cast, and a reified wrapper that stores its lambda needs noinline.
A typed key carries its value's type (Key<T> with a KType inside), so reads need no cast and same-named keys of different types don't collide.
A key is used to write, so it must be invariant. With out T, a wrong value goes in and fails later as a ClassCastException.
The limit: these designs check types, not meaning, and the board rings only for the exact class. When a design needs much more, a sealed class and a when are often plainer.

explain.prompt: A teammate reviews the lab's BellBoard and asks two things: why the board wraps every listener in a lambda instead of storing it directly, and why the stock-keeper, typed (Fruit) -> Unit, can listen under Apple::class. Explain both with the producer and consumer picture.
explain.answer: Deliveries are produced at the back door and consumed by listeners, so a listener's type is in on its parameter. That gives both answers. A listener typed (Apple) -> Unit can only consume apples, so it is not a (Fruit) -> Unit, which must consume any fruit. The board keeps one list of (Fruit) -> Unit per class, so it can't store the apple listener as it is. It stores an adapter instead: a function that takes any Fruit, checks it with Apple::class.safeCast, and passes it on only if it really is an apple. Casting the listener would compile, but it would fail with a ClassCastException inside the listener the first time a lemon arrived. The stock-keeper goes the other way. It consumes every Fruit, so it can certainly consume apples. Because the parameter is in, a (Fruit) -> Unit is an (Apple) -> Unit, and listen(Apple::class, stockCount) type-checks with E = Apple.

deeper.html:
Each design has a natural next step.

The board rings only for the item's exact class. To ring a listener under Fruit::class for an apple too, ring must walk the item's supertypes. Without kotlin-reflect you can do that through Java reflection: item.javaClass.interfaces and item.javaClass.superclass, converted with .kotlin. With kotlin-reflect, KClass.allSuperclasses lists them directly. Cache the result per class, since the walk is the same every time.

Either gets more useful with flatMap, which chains steps that can each fail: fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.flatMap(f: (R) -> Either<L, R2>): Either<L, R2>. Its Left branch returns this for the same reason map can. The standard library's own Result<out T> is declared out too, but its failure side is always a Throwable; Either lets the problem be a type of your own, such as a DeliveryProblem. Libraries such as Arrow ship a full Either.

The storeroom can grow a write-only view as well: interface Intake<in T> { fun save(item: T) }. A loader that writes Suppliers can then accept an Intake<Item<Long>>. With both views, the invariant Storeroom is simply the type that is both.

The typed keys can carry a default: class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType, val default: T), with get returning T instead of T?. Keep Key invariant when you do: default is read, but set still writes through the key.
